summary: Defines an IMAP4 extension for non-synchronizing literals, so a client can send large pieces of data without waiting for the server's go-ahead each time. It was replaced by RFC 7888.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of asking each time if you can keep talking, you keep talking and the server keeps up.

questions: what is a non-synchronizing literal in imap
how does imap literal plus save a round trip
subtitle: Let an IMAP client send a string without pausing for the server's go-ahead.

tldr.problem: In IMAP4, a client sending a literal must wait for the server's command continuation request between the octet count and the string data, which costs a network round trip.
tldr.mechanism: A non-synchronizing literal puts a plus sign between the octet count and the closing brace, as in {11+}, and the client sends the data right away. Servers advertise support with the LITERAL+ capability.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2088 has been obsoleted by RFC 7888.

today: RFC 2088 is obsoleted by RFC 7888, and it was updated by RFC 4466. Use the newer specification.

sections.title: The Round Trip Problem
sections.content:
The Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP4) has a syntactic construct called a literal for sending strings. When a client sends one, IMAP4 requires it to wait for the server to send a command continuation request between the octet count and the string data.

This document defines an alternate form of literal that does not need this network round trip. The original form is then called a synchronizing literal.
sections.plainLanguage: Each time the client wants to send a long string, it has to stop and wait for a thumbs-up. That waiting is slow.

sections.title: The Plus Sign Form
sections.content:
A non-synchronizing literal may be sent from client to server instead of the normal form. It is marked by a plus (+) between the octet count and the closing brace. The server does not send a continuation request for it, and the client need not wait before sending the octets.

A client may use it only with a server that lists LITERAL+ in its response to the CAPABILITY command. Otherwise the client must use synchronizing literals.

The server must check the end of every received line for an open brace, an octet count, a plus and a close brace right before the CRLF. When it finds that, it MUST treat the stated number of following octets and the next line as part of the same command. It MAY still process commands and reject errors line by line, as long as it checks each line end.
sections.plainLanguage: A little plus sign says "I am not waiting, here it comes". The client may only do this if the server said earlier that it understands the plus sign.

sections.title: Example and Grammar
sections.content:
The RFC's example is a LOGIN command in which both the user name and the password are sent as non-synchronizing literals, with no server prompts in between.

The formal syntax, in augmented BNF, changes the literal rule so that the + is optional: an open brace, a number, an optional plus, a close brace, CRLF, then the octets. The RFC reports no known security issues with the extension.
sections.plainLanguage: In the example, the client sends a name and a password back to back, and the server just says the login worked.
